relations.subject: index:covering-index
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the page's lede makes early filtering the fallback, not an alternative
relations.evidence: When covering indexes and index pushdowns are not available, the Query Service may use early filtering, early ordering, and early pagination to improve the query response time.

relations.subject: index:index-pushdown
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - and the Limitations section states the precedence as a hard condition, not a preference
relations.evidence: Index pushdown for `ORDER`, `LIMIT` and `OFFSET` must not be possible.

relations.subject: index:covering-index
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: If a query has a [covering index](covering-indexes.md), and the query is on a single keyspace, then the index contains all the data needed to perform the query. The Query service does not need to fetch data from the Data service. Any filters, order, or pagination (offset and limit) are performed by the Index service.

relations.subject: service:query-service
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the default, non-covered path: fetch first, then filter
relations.evidence: If a query is _not_ covered by an index, then the query needs to fetch data from the Data service after performing the index scan, in order to return the requested results. By default, any filters, order, or pagination are performed by the Query service after the fetch.

relations.subject: index:early-filtering
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the page states the fetch cost as the thing every one of the four methods is trading against
relations.evidence: Fetching data from the Data service can be expensive. Any feature that can reduce the amount of data to be fetched will improve the query response time.

relations.subject: index:index-pushdown
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: Some filters, ordering, and pagination may be pushed down to the Index service, along with grouping and aggregates. The Index service applies these operations to the result of the index scan.

relations.subject: index:group-aggregate-pushdown

relations.evidence: Some filters, ordering, and pagination may be pushed down to the Index service, along with grouping and aggregates. The Index service applies these operations to the result of the index scan.

relations.subject: index:predicate-pushdown
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused
relations.evidence: However, there are some operations that cannot be pushed down to the Index service: for example, a filter that uses a function or a LIKE operator on top of an index term. These operations must be performed by the Query service.

relations.subject: index:early-filtering
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - the load-bearing distinction from a pushdown: the work is still done by the Query service, only earlier
relations.evidence: In Couchbase Capella, _early filtering_, _early ordering_, and _early pagination_ provide another line of defense, in cases where covering indexes and index pushdowns are not available. With this feature, the Query service may apply filtering, ordering, and pagination directly to the results returned by the Index service, before performing the fetch.

notable_absence.finding: There is no way to turn early filtering, early ordering or early pagination on or off, and the page never says so explicitly - it simply never mentions a setting, a request parameter or an optimizer hint anywhere in 550 lines, and attributes every decision to the optimizer ('The optimizer only selects early ordering and pagination when the following conditions are met'). So the correct relation here is an absence, not an offersConfigurationChoice: this is a feature the user can only influence by index design and query shape. Contrast index_pushdowns.md, which is the same kind of page and equally settingless, with groupby-aggregate-performance.md, which at least offers a query rewrite as a workaround for the FILTER-clause limitation. Also absent: the Limitations section lists eight conditions for early ORDERING and pagination and none at all for early FILTERING, even though the body of the page shows early filtering has its own condition (the filter must be evaluable on the index keys). A reader cannot tell from this page when early filtering will not happen.

cross_component_finding: This page is the corpus's clearest evidence that the four mechanisms in this batch form one ranked family, and its Summary table states the ranking outright, in four columns - covering index / index pushdown / early filters, order, or pagination / default - crossed with two rows, 'Fetch required?' (No / Yes / Yes / Yes) and the service that performs the work (Index service / Index service / Query service / Query service). That is a two-axis classification of the whole family, and I could not encode it as relations without inventing an ordering predicate, so it is recorded here verbatim for phase 2, which may want a `plan-strategy:` enum or an `isMoreEfficientThan` chain. The distinguishing axis is not efficiency but WHERE the work happens: pushdown moves work to the Index service, early filtering keeps it in the Query service and only moves it earlier. Second finding, an id defect: the corpus holds two spellings for both of this page's concepts - index:early-filtering (used by this page's record and by server/8.0/indexes/covering-indexes.json) and n1ql:early-filtering (used by server/7.2/learn/services-and-indexes/indexes/early-filters-and-pagination.json, the Server copy of this very page), likewise index:early-order-and-pagination and n1ql:early-order-and-pagination. Two spellings of one concept split its recurrence count in half and make it invisible to promotion. I reused the index: pair because it has two citations to the n1ql: pair's one, but the namespace argument actually favours n1ql: here: the page insists this work is done BY THE QUERY SERVICE, which is precisely what distinguishes it from a pushdown. Phase 2 must merge these, and the same question decides the pushdown-family spelling flagged in cloud/indexes/index_pushdowns.json.
cross_product_finding: 'In Couchbase Capella, _early filtering_, _early ordering_, and _early pagination_ provide another line of defense' is a Server release-note sentence with the version removed and the product name swapped - the Server 7.6 copy of this page dates the feature, and this one cannot. So no availableSince relation is extractable from the Capella copy of a feature page, ever, and phase 2 should expect version facts about Capella features to be sourced only from the Server tree. Note also that this page is the only one of the five that links out to the SQL++ clause reference pages (WHERE, ORDER BY, OFFSET, LIMIT) with an explicit gloss of what each is for ('— to apply a filter', '— to apply a sort', '— to apply pagination'), which makes it the natural bridge record between the indexes/ and n1ql/ subtrees.
